your-first-program.proof: A program that prints the exact line "Hello, world!" — run it yourself and read the output it produced.
your-first-program.unlock: Your program runs and prints the exact required line, with no typos.
your-first-program.outcome: Write and run your very first program: make the computer print an exact line of text on screen, and understand the edit → run → see-output loop that every programmer lives in.
your-first-program.doNotClaim: Don't claim you "ran code" until you've actually pressed Run and SEEN your line appear in the output — reading about it is not the same as running it.

your-first-program.text: Right now the computer does nothing you tell it — because you have never told it anything. In the next twenty minutes you type one line, press Run, and watch a machine do exactly what you said.
Everything you will ever build is just instructions you write and the computer runs, one after another. The whole job rests on one loop: edit, run, see, adjust.

your-first-program.prompt: Before you read on: a friend says "the computer is smart — it figures out what I mean." You type an instruction with a small typo. What do you think happens?
your-first-program.reveal: The computer does NOT guess what you meant — it does exactly what you typed, or it stops and complains. That is the most important thing to learn first: the computer is precise, not smart. A typo is not "close enough"; it is wrong, and the program will tell you. This is good news — it means the rules are consistent, and you are always in control.

storyboard.say: Everything you build starts here. You write an instruction the computer will follow, like print with your words in quotes.
You hand those instructions to the machine and press Run. It executes your lines top to bottom, exactly as written.
Running produces output. For your first program, that is your quoted text printed back on the screen.
Now you compare what you see to what you wanted. This is the moment you decide whether it did the job.
If it is off, you go back and try again, changing the instruction and running it once more.
That is the whole job: edit, run, see, adjust, round and round. Master this loop and you can build anything.

your-first-program.text: Here is the habit that separates people who get unstuck fast from people who panic: an error is not the computer scolding you — it is the computer telling you exactly where it got confused. variables-and-values.proof: A program that stores a computed total in a variable and prints it — the right number appears in the output.
variables-and-values.unlock: Your variable holds the correct value and your program prints it.
variables-and-values.outcome: Store a value in a named variable, change it by reassigning, and use a variable in a calculation — so your programs can remember and reuse values instead of repeating them.
variables-and-values.doNotClaim: Don't claim you "understand variables" until your program has STORED a value in a name and used that name again later — not just printed a number directly.

variables-and-values.text: In Lesson 1 you printed a line — then the computer forgot it instantly. Real programs remember: a score that climbs, a total built from parts. Today you give a value a name you can hold onto and reuse.

A variable is the most-used thing in all of programming — every score, total, and result lives in one. Master "store under a name, then use the name" and every later topic is just variables being read and changed.

variables-and-values.prompt: Before you read on: you write  score = 0  and later  score = 10. After both lines run, what is in  score — 0, 10, or both?
variables-and-values.reveal: It is 10. A variable holds ONE value at a time — the most recent one assigned to it. The second line replaces the first; the 0 is gone. A variable is a labelled box, not a list of everything ever put in it. This "the latest value wins" rule is exactly what lets a score go up or a total change as your program runs.

variables-and-values.text: Create one with assignment: name = value. The single = stores the right side into the name on the left (not math "equals"). Use the name to read its current value; assign again and the new value replaces the old.
variables-and-values.title: A variable is a name that holds a value

variables-and-values.code:
price = 20          # store 20 under the name "price"
print(price)        # use the name -> shows 20
price = price - 5   # compute the right side, store it back
print(price)        # the name now holds 15 -> shows 15

steps.note: price = 20 puts the value 20 into the name price. The single = means "store", not "is equal to".
steps.label: Assignment stores a value

steps.note: print(price) substitutes the current value of price → shows 20.
steps.label: Read by using the name

steps.note: Compute 20 - 5 = 15, THEN store 15 back into price. The old 20 is replaced — a variable holds only its latest value.
steps.label: Right side first, then store

steps.note: print(price) now shows 15. The name followed the latest assignment.
steps.label: Same name, new value

storyboard.say: Start on the right side: per_box times boxes. The computer works out this value first, before anything gets a name.
The single equals sign is the store arrow. It drops the finished right-side value into the box on the left.
That box has a label: total_eggs. The name is written on the outside, the computed value sleeps inside.
Later, saying the name reads the box. total_eggs substitutes its current contents, eighteen, wherever you use it.
So print of total_eggs shows 18, because reading the name just hands back whatever value is stored inside.
The whole loop: compute a value, store it under a name, then read the name to reuse it. That is a variable.

A good name is not neatness — it is how code stays readable long after you have forgotten writing it.

numbers-and-strings.proof: A program that combines numbers and text into one exact formatted line and prints it.
numbers-and-strings.unlock: Your line matches the required output exactly, with the numbers computed (not hardcoded into the text).
numbers-and-strings.outcome: Tell numbers and text apart, do arithmetic on numbers, convert between text and numbers when you need to, and build a clean formatted line by dropping values into text with an f-string.
numbers-and-strings.doNotClaim: Don't claim you "get types" until you've seen with your own eyes that "2" + "3" is "23" but 2 + 3 is 5 — the difference is the whole lesson.

numbers-and-strings.text: In Lesson 2 you added numbers and it just worked. So this will rattle you: add two quantities and get "23" instead of 5 — because your values have a hidden property called a type, and text and numbers obey different rules under the same + sign.

Every value has a type, and the type decides what an operation means: numbers add, text joins. Input from forms, files, and the keyboard arrives as TEXT even when it looks like a number — so telling them apart and converting is foundational.

numbers-and-strings.prompt: Before you read on: what do you think  "2" + "3"  gives — and what does  2 + 3  give? Are they the same?
numbers-and-strings.reveal: 2 + 3 is 5 (numbers add). But "2" + "3" is "23" — with quotes they are TEXT, and + on text means "join end to end" (concatenation), not "add". Same symbol, different meaning, decided entirely by the TYPE of the values. Text that looks like a number is still text until you convert it.

numbers-and-strings.intro: Compute on numbers, format with an f-string. Do the math first, then drop the values into text with { }.
numbers-and-strings.code:
price = 4
qty = 3
total = price * qty          # numbers -> arithmetic -> 12 (an int)

line = f"Total for {qty} items: ${total}"
print(line)                  # -> Total for 3 items: $12
steps: These are numbers (int): No quotes, so price and qty are ints — ready for arithmetic.
Multiply the numbers: price * qty does real multiplication → 12, an int.
An f-string starts with f: The f before the opening quote turns on substitution; anything in { } is evaluated and dropped in.
Only the { } parts get replaced: {qty} → 3, {total} → 12. The dollar sign and words are plain text. Numbers become text automatically here.
Print the finished line: Output: Total for 3 items: $12 — numbers computed, then formatted.
numbers-and-strings.commonMistake: This is supposed to add two quantities and show 5, but it prints 23.

numbers-and-strings.text: int is a whole number (4); float has a decimal (3.14); str is text in quotes ("4"). The type decides what + means — numbers add, strings join. Convert deliberately: int("4") gives 4; str(4) gives "4".

numbers-and-strings.title: Converting across the type boundary
numbers-and-strings.subtitle: Text that looks numeric is str until int() crosses it over; str() crosses a number back to text.

storyboard.say: Start here: "25" in quotes is a string — text that only looks like a number, so plus would join it, not add it.
To do math, you cross the type boundary: int("25") reads the digits and hands back a real whole number.
Now it's the number 25 — a true int, so 25 + 1 gives 26, because plus on numbers means add.
Going the other way, str(25) crosses the same boundary back, turning the number into the text "25".
Back as a string, plus now joins instead of adds — so it can concatenate cleanly with other text.
The core insight: the type, not the character, decides what plus means — so convert deliberately every time.

numbers-and-strings.text: Reach for an f-string whenever you mix text and values: f"{name} scored {points}". It is cleaner and less error-prone than gluing pieces with + and str(), and it makes the final line obvious at a glance. Just remember the leading f — without it, the { } show up literally as characters.

reading-input.proof: A program that reads a name and a count from input, then prints one exact formatted line built from both — the numbers used as numbers, not text.
reading-input.unlock: Your program reads the provided input and prints the exact required line, with the count converted to a real number.
reading-input.outcome: Make your program RECEIVE data instead of only using values you typed in: read a line with input(), convert it to a number with int() when you need to do math, and print an exact line built from what you read.
reading-input.doNotClaim: Don't claim you "read input" until your program has taken a line from input(), converted the numeric one with int(), and printed the exact line built from BOTH — printing a value you hardcoded is not reading input.

reading-input.text: Every program you have written already knew its answer — you typed it in. A real program does not know who is using it; it has to ask. Today your program stops talking to itself and starts listening.

Reading input is the front door of almost every program — a login form, a search box, a number from a file. The shape is always the same: pull in a value, convert it (input arrives as TEXT), then use it.

reading-input.prompt: Before you read on: a user types  3  and you read it with  count = input(). You then write  count + 1  to get 4. What actually happens?
reading-input.reveal: It does NOT give 4 — it errors. input() ALWAYS hands back text, so count is the string "3", not the number 3. And you cannot add a number to text, so  "3" + 1  stops with a TypeError. This is the catch that gets every beginner: a thing that LOOKS like a number on screen is still text until you convert it. Wrap it in int() first — count = int(input()) — and then count + 1 is 4. Read as text, convert before you do math.

reading-input.intro: Read · convert · use. Two lines come in as text; only the numeric one is converted. Watch where int() goes.
reading-input.code:
name = input()              # reads a line -> text, e.g. "Sam"
age_text = input()          # reads the next line -> text, e.g. "30"
age = int(age_text)         # convert that text to a real number -> 30

print(f"Hi {name}, next year you turn {age + 1}.")
steps: First input() → text: Reads one line and returns it as a string; name becomes "Sam". The prompt argument, if any, is just a hint — not part of the value.
Second input() → next line: Each call reads the NEXT line in order; age_text becomes the text "30".
Convert the numeric one: int(age_text) crosses the text "30" into the number 30, stored in age.
Now arithmetic works: Because age is a real number, age + 1 → 31 (on text it would error). The f-string drops name and 31 into the sentence.
reading-input.commonMistake: This should read a count and print "You have 4 items." (3 typed, plus 1), but it crashes with a TypeError instead.

reading-input.text: input() reads one line the user provides and hands it back as a string — always text. Convert when you need a number: int(input()) turns "3" into 3. It is the "2" vs 2 type difference from Lesson 3, at the boundary.
reading-input.title: input() reads a line as text; convert with int() to get a number

reading-input.title: Input crosses the boundary as text
reading-input.subtitle: Outside the program everything is text. Convert at the door, then the rest of the program can trust real numbers.

storyboard.say: It starts outside the program: a person at the keyboard types 3 and presses enter. The program does not know this value yet.
input() opens the front door. It reads exactly one line the user provides and hands that line back to your program.
Here is the catch: whatever comes through that door is text. Typing 3 gives you the string "3", never the number.
So you convert at the boundary. int(...) takes the string "3" and turns it into a real number you can do math with.
Now it is the number 3. Add one and you get 4 — arithmetic that would have failed on the raw text.

loops.text: Last lesson you built a list that can hold a hundred values. Picture writing a hundred lines to add them up. That is not programming; that is typing. A loop says "do this for every item" exactly once.

Looping is how every program handles "for each": total each line of a receipt, email each user, draw each enemy. Bring along the if from Lesson 5 and you can count, filter, and decide across a whole dataset.

loops.prompt: Before you read on: you want to add up [10, 20, 30]. You write  total = 0  before a loop that does  total = total + price  for each price. Why does total have to start at 0 BEFORE the loop, not inside it?
loops.reveal: Because the loop body runs once per item, and you want to keep adding onto the same running total. If total = 0 were inside the loop, it would reset to 0 on every pass and wipe out your progress — you would end with just the last value. Setting it to 0 once, before the loop, gives you an empty bucket; each pass pours one more value in. Start outside, accumulate inside.

storyboard.say: Before the loop even starts, we set up one bucket: total = 0. This happens once, outside the repetition.
We hand the empty bucket to the loop and start marching through nums, one value at a time.
For each item, n takes the next value and we drop into the loop body to do the work.
Inside, we update the SAME bucket: total = total + n. We never make a new total, we add onto it.
Then we loop back for the next item, and the bucket carries its running value forward each pass.
When nums runs out, the loop exits and the bucket holds the finished answer: total = 20.
That is the accumulator pattern: initialise outside once, accumulate inside every pass, read the result when done.

functions-basics.proof: A program that defines a function, calls it with arguments, and prints a computed result that the function returned.
functions-basics.unlock: Your function takes inputs, returns the right value, and your program prints it via that returned value.
functions-basics.outcome: Define your own function with def, give it inputs (parameters), send a value back with return, and call it to reuse a block of code — so you stop copy-pasting the same steps and start naming them.
functions-basics.doNotClaim: Don't claim you "understand functions" until your program has DEFINED a function, CALLED it with arguments, and used the value it RETURNED — printing inside the function without ever returning is not the whole skill.

functions-basics.text: Look back: a loop that totals a list, an if that grades a score. Useful — but each lives in one spot. A function lets you name a block of code once and run it on demand, with different inputs every time.

Functions are how every program stays manageable: small named pieces — calculate_total, is_valid — snapped together. Naming a step makes code readable; reusing it kills copy-paste bugs. Every library you import is just someone else's functions.

functions-basics.prompt: Before you read on: a function does  print(unit_price * qty)  but has no return. You write  bill = total_price(7, 6)  and then  print(bill). What ends up in  bill — the number 42, or something else?
functions-basics.reveal: bill is None — NOT 42. print() shows a value on screen but does not hand it BACK to the caller. To get a value out of a function so you can store and reuse it, the function must return it. A function that only prints can show you something; a function that returns gives you something. This difference — print vs return — is the single most important idea in this lesson.

functions-basics.intro: Define once, call many. Watch the arguments fill the parameters and the value come back to the caller.
functions-basics.code:
def area(width, height):     # width and height are parameters (inputs)
    return width * height    # hand the result back to the caller

room = area(3, 4)            # arguments 3, 4 fill width, height -> returns 12
print(room)                  # -> 12

print(area(10, 2))           # call again with new inputs -> returns 20
steps: def names the function: Two parameters, width and height — placeholders for the inputs the caller supplies. Nothing runs yet; defining is not calling.
return hands a value back: Computes width * height and sends it to whoever called the function, ending it.
Calling fills the parameters: area(3, 4): the arguments 3 and 4 fill width and height in order; the call becomes the returned 12.
Store and use the result: room = area(3, 4) stores 12, so print(room) shows 12. The call evaluates to its return value.
Reuse with new inputs: area(10, 2) runs the SAME function again → 20. One definition, many calls — the whole point.
functions-basics.commonMistake: This should print 42, but it prints None instead.

functions-basics.text: def total_price(unit_price, qty): names a function; the names in parentheses are parameters. return sends a value back to the caller and ends the function. Call it with arguments — total_price(7, 6) — and the call becomes whatever was returned.

How a function call works
functions-basics.subtitle: Arguments flow in to fill the parameters; the function runs; return flows the result back out.

storyboard.say: It starts with a call: area(3, 4). You name the function and hand it two arguments, 3 and 4.
Those arguments flow in to fill the parameters — width becomes 3, height becomes 4.
With its parameters filled, the function body runs the code you named once and can reuse anywhere.
The body computes width times height, using whatever inputs it was given this time.
Then return sends the result back — return 12 hands a value to the caller and ends the function.
The result flows back out, and the call itself becomes 12 — that's the whole loop of a function.

build-a-tiny-program.proof: A single working program that defines a function, loops over a list with a decision inside, and prints two exact lines computed from the data (a passing count and an average).
build-a-tiny-program.unlock: Your program runs end to end and prints both required lines, with every number computed from the data — nothing hardcoded.
build-a-tiny-program.outcome: Combine everything from First Steps — a variable, a list, a loop, an if, and a function — into ONE small program that processes real in-code data and prints a useful result. This is your first genuinely shipped program.
build-a-tiny-program.doNotClaim: Don't claim you "shipped a program" until it RUNS top to bottom and prints both correct lines from the data — a program that prints the right numbers only because you typed them in is not the skill.

build-a-tiny-program.text: Seven lessons ago you could not print a line. Today none of it is practice: you snap print, variables, types, decisions, lists, loops, and functions into one real program — a tiny gradebook that reports how many passed and the class average.

Every real program is the basics combined: take data, loop over it, decide, compute, report. A bank statement, a leaderboard, a sales report — same shape. Holding several pieces at once and wiring them together is what "can build" means.

build-a-tiny-program.prompt: Before you read on: you need a passing COUNT and a running TOTAL from one list. Do you need two separate loops over the scores, or can one loop do both jobs at the same time?
build-a-tiny-program.reveal: One loop is enough — and better. On each pass you can add the score to your total AND, with an if, bump the passing count when it qualifies. Two accumulators (total = 0 and passed = 0) set up before the loop, both updated inside the same loop, both ready when it ends. Looping the data twice would work but wastes effort; real programs do as much as they can in one well-organised pass.

build-a-tiny-program.intro: The gradebook, every line earning its place. One program — variable, list, loop, if, function — working as a team.
build-a-tiny-program.code:
def summarize(scores):
    total = 0
    passed = 0
    for s in scores:             # one pass over the data
        total = total + s        # running total
        if s >= 60:              # decision
            passed = passed + 1  # count the passes
    print(f"Passed: {passed} of {len(scores)}")
    return total / len(scores)   # hand back the average

scores = [40, 80, 95, 50, 85]
avg = summarize(scores)
print(f"Average: {int(avg)}")    # -> Passed: 3 of 5 / Average: 70
steps: Wrap the job in a function (L8): summarize(scores) names the whole task and lets you reuse it on any list of scores.
Two accumulators, set up first (L2 & L7): total and passed created BEFORE the loop — the empty buckets. Inside the loop they would reset every pass.
One loop, running total (L7): Walk the list once; total grows on every pass.
A decision inside the loop (L5): The if counts only scores >= 60 — loop and if working together.
Compute and report after (L1, L3, L8): After the loop: print the count, then return the average (total / len). The caller prints it with an f-string and int(avg).

storyboard.say: Every real program has one shape: take data, loop over it, decide, compute, report. Here it's a tiny gradebook of scores.
Before the loop, set up empty result holders: total starts at zero, passed starts at zero. Nothing counted yet.
Now the data feeds the loop. We walk the list one score at a time until every item is seen.
For each score we do two things: add it to the total, and use an if to check whether it passed.
The decision — if the score is sixty or more — bumps the passed count; then we loop back for the next item.
When the list runs out, the loop is done and we exit it to compute the final figures.
After the loop we divide total by length to get the average, then print and return the result — one reusable function.

input-validation.text: Your signup endpoint just accepted an empty email, a 50,000-character name, and age = -3 — and that garbage is now in your database. The gradebook you shipped in First Steps worked only because its data was clean; real data never is. Today your code stops trusting input and checks it at the boundary first.
Unchecked input is the #1 cause of crashes, corrupted data, and a whole class of security bugs. It is the through-line of this module: distrust the outside world, check it at the edge.

input-validation.prompt: Before you read on: a teammate says "the frontend already validates the form, so the API doesn't need to." Why is that dangerous?
input-validation.reveal: The client is untrusted. Anyone can call the API directly — curl, a script, a malicious client — and skip the UI entirely. Validation must happen server-side, at the boundary. Client validation is only a UX nicety; it is never a security control.

input-validation.intro: The boundary pattern, one check at a time. Parse into a known shape, then check type → presence → length → range, rejecting with an actionable error.
steps: Shape first: Parse into a known shape before trusting any field. If it is not even a dict, reject immediately.
Presence + type: `data.get("email")` is missing-safe; the isinstance check rejects non-strings before you ever call a string method.
Length (stops DoS / overflow): A 50,000-char name is a denial-of-service vector. Bound it at the edge.
Range: age = -3 is the bug from the mission. isinstance(age, int) also blocks the hostile string "25".
Normalize only when safe: Return a clean shape; `.strip()` is an explicit, safe transform — never silently coerce a wrong type.
input-validation.commonMistake: This "validator" accepts the string "25" and even -3 silently — bad data flows downstream.

input-validation.text: A trust boundary is any line where untrusted data crosses into your system. At that edge, confirm shape → type → presence → range → length → rules before the system believes a word of it. Reject by default; normalize only when the transform is safe and explicit.
input-validation.title: Input is hostile until proven valid
Where validation lives — at the boundary, before any side effect
input-validation.subtitle: Untrusted input must pass the validator before it can touch the database. Validate first, act second.

storyboard.say: Everything starts here: untrusted input arrives from the outside world, and you cannot assume any of it is well-formed.
That input crosses the trust boundary and hits the validator first, before it can touch anything real inside your system.
At the edge the validator checks shape, type, presence, range, length, and rules, deciding one thing: is this data trustworthy?
If anything fails, the request is rejected immediately, so an empty email or an age of minus three never gets any further.
Only valid, checked data is allowed through to your application logic, which can now trust every field it receives.
Because the data was cleaned at the boundary, the write to the database stores only trustworthy values, not garbage.
The core insight: validate first, act second. Guard the boundary once and every layer behind it stays clean.

error-handling.text: A background job has been "succeeding" for a week — because it wrapped everything in `except Exception: pass`. Thousands of records silently failed and no one knew. Last lesson you rejected bad input at the door; today you handle the failures that slip past every guard, making them loud, safe, and diagnosable.
Error handling is where junior and senior code diverge. The same try/except can hide a production outage for a week or turn it into a 30-second fix.

error-handling.prompt: Before you read on: why is `except Exception: pass` one of the most dangerous lines you can write?
error-handling.reveal: It swallows EVERY error — including ones you never anticipated (a real bug, disk-full, a typo). The program keeps running as if nothing happened, so the failure becomes invisible and undebuggable. Catch narrowly, handle deliberately, and never silently pass.

error-handling.intro: Catch deliberately — one branch at a time. Specific catches, operator context logged, a safe user message, retry only where it is safe.
steps: The risky call: Only the line that can fail goes in the try. Wrapping more would catch bugs you meant to let crash.
Transient → retryable: A network blip is recoverable. Log operator context, then re-raise a typed RetryableError — retry only if the call is idempotent.
Declined → non-retryable: Retrying a declined card just fails again. Surface a safe user message; log the real error for the operator.
Chain with `from e`: Python keeps the original as `__cause__`, so the operator sees the true root cause — not just your wrapper.
error-handling.commonMistake: This "handles" errors — and hid a week of silent data loss.

error-handling.text: Good error handling answers four questions: recoverable or fatal? retryable or not? what does the USER safely see? what does the OPERATOR need logged? Safe failure = the system fails in a known, observable state — loudly, with context — never silently.
error-handling.title: Recoverable vs fatal · user message vs operator context
An error arrives — classify, then act
error-handling.subtitle: Every failure routes through the same four questions. A bare `except: pass` short-circuits all of them.

storyboard.say: An exception is raised — but here it's caught narrowly, at the door, not swallowed by a blanket except.
First question: is this recoverable or fatal? Every failure routes through this one decision.
If it's fatal, don't hide it — let it surface loudly so the system fails in a known, observable state.
If it's recoverable, ask the next question: is this the kind of error worth retrying?
Either way, always log operator context — the trace and detail an engineer needs to fix it fast.
Then give the user a safe message — no leaked internals — and surface the failure honestly.
A bare except-pass short-circuits all four questions — that's how a background job silently fails for a week.

functions-and-modules.outcome: Write a small, single-purpose, PURE function with a clear signature — and a test that proves it — then refactor a side-effecting function to be testable.
functions-and-modules.doNotClaim: Don't claim mastery until you've turned a function that reads a global / prints into a pure one that returns a value, with a test.

functions-and-modules.text: Your `calculate_total()` works perfectly when you run it by hand, then its tests fail at random for no reason you can see — because it reads a global `cart` and prints instead of returning. Today you make it small, pure, and predictable enough that a test is just one line.
Functions are the unit of reuse AND the unit of testing. Small, single-purpose, predictable functions are why some codebases are a joy and others a minefield.

functions-and-modules.prompt: Before you read on: why is a function that reads a global variable harder to test than one that takes everything as a parameter?
functions-and-modules.reveal: A function that depends on hidden global state behaves differently depending on what ran before it — tests become order-dependent and flaky. A function that takes its inputs as parameters and returns a value (a pure function) gives the same output for the same input every time, so a test is just `assert f(x) == expected`.

functions-and-modules.intro: A module: related functions behind one interface. Group the pure functions in a file; other code imports the contract, not the internals.
steps: The smallest pure unit: `line_total` does one job: price * qty. Nothing hidden, nothing printed.
Compose, do not repeat: `cart_total` reuses `line_total` — small pure pieces wired together, each testable alone.
Import the contract: main.py pulls in only `cart_total`. It depends on the interface, not the internals.
The caller does the I/O: Printing lives here, OUTSIDE the pure functions — so the core stays deterministic and reusable.
functions-and-modules.commonMistake: This function "works" in the REPL but its test is flaky — it passes or fails depending on what ran first.

functions-and-modules.text: Its name says what it does, its parameters declare what it needs, its return value is what it promises. PURE functions (output depends only on inputs, no side effects) are trivial to test and reuse. A MODULE groups related functions behind a clear interface.
functions-and-modules.title: A function is a contract: name · inputs · output · one job
Pure vs impure — what a test can actually pin down
functions-and-modules.subtitle: A pure function depends only on its arguments. An impure one also reads hidden state, so the same call can return different answers.

storyboard.say: A pure function is a promise: its parameters declare everything it needs, and nothing else can reach in.
Because the arguments are all it sees, the same inputs always produce the same return value. Deterministic.
That is why a pure function is trivial to test: one line, one call, one expected answer, no setup.
Now the impure twin. It still takes your declared arguments, but that is only half the story.
It also secretly reads global state, a hidden input your function signature never mentions.
So the same call returns different answers depending on that hidden state, and your test fails at random.
The fix is not more tests, it is fewer hidden inputs: make the function pure and the flakiness disappears.

# changes `discount`. Refactor line_total to be PURE: depend ONLY on its

print(f"pure (survives a changed global): {pure}")
print(f"PASS: {correct and pure}")

storyboard.say: The loop starts at index zero, processing the first active order. The cursor sits on i=0 and everything looks fine.
The cursor advances to index one, where it finds a cancelled order that we've decided to remove.
We call remove() on the cancelled item at index one, deleting it from the list in place.
Here's the trap: removing index one shifts every later item left, so what was index two now becomes index one.
But the cursor still advances to index two, skipping right over the item that just slid into slot one, unseen.
That's how a loop meant to remove all cancelled orders silently leaves half of them behind.
The fix is simple: never mutate while iterating. Build a new list of the items you want to keep instead.

storyboard.say: A nightly job leaks handles and crashes on a missing config. The fix starts here: with open(path) claims the file under a context manager.
The first thing the outside world can break is existence. We try to open, and ask: is the file even there?
If the file is missing, open raises — but the context manager still runs its exit, so the handle is released, not leaked.
On the happy path the file opened, so we stream it: for line in f, one line at a time, never loading gigabytes into memory.
Per line, a new risk appears: a parse or encoding error mid-stream. Surface it, don't swallow it.
Whether that line raises an error or the loop finishes cleanly, both paths land at the same place: the handle gets closed.
That's the lesson: with guarantees the close on every exit — success, error, or missing file. A bare open only cleans up on the happy path.

steps: The edge the happy path forgot: An empty list short-circuits to 0 — `sum([]) / len([])` would be 0/0, a ZeroDivisionError.
The normal computation: Only reached once the edge is handled. Order matters: guard first, compute second.
Assert behavior, not internals: Normal and single-element cases. We check input → output, so a refactor of the body cannot break the test.
The regression case: The empty list — the exact input that crashed prod. This line is why the bug can never silently return.

storyboard.say: It starts here: an atomic commit is one logical change, small enough that you could revert it on its own.
Because the change is isolated, git revert can cleanly undo just that one commit without touching everything else.
The same discipline lets git bisect binary-search your history to pinpoint exactly which commit introduced a bug.

Here's the risk: force-pushing a shared branch rewrites history others rely on, defeating revert, bisect, and reflog at once.
The insight: keep commits small and never force-push shared branches, and any mistake becomes a thirty-second recovery.
